newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean Kim apologises "in agony" for scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean Kim apologises "in agony" for scandal.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam apologised in "agony and sorrow" on Tuesday for a loan scandal that has put three of his close associates in custody and rocked the nation.

Appearing chastened and solemn in a televised address on the fourth anniversary of his inauguration, Kim also said he was shamed by his second son being embroiled in the scandal swirling around the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
"The whole nation is now swept by shocks from the Hanbo incident," said white-haired Kim, his eyes downcast as he read from a prepared text in the 18-minute address.

"I have travelled a one-way road with self-restraint and abstinence in the past four years and am devastated and in despair," he said, referring to an anti-corruption drive he launched shortly after taking office in 1993.

State prosecutors last week indicted 10 people, including a cabinet minister, prominent politicians from ruling and opposition parties, top bankers and the founder of the Hanbo Group, the country's 14th largest conglomerate.
Kim's son, Hyun-chul, was questioned over the weekend in connection with the affair but cleared of any wrongdoing.
Kim said he would bar his son, aged 38, from social activities until the end of his five-year presidential term next February.

"Whatever the reasons, all these are the consequence of my lack of virtue. It is the responsibility of myself, the president," Kim said. He said he would humbly accept all reprimands and criticism by the people.

"I, as the president, offer a sincere apology to the people over this incident," he said in a low monotone in striking contrast to his combative last television appearance a month ago when he laid the blame on his opponents.
Kim's speech had little immediate impact on the financial markets, with the key stock market index rising 2.65 points to 679.24 and then falling to around 675 in 30 minutes.
Kim said he would not retreat from reform policies, now in tatters, after the scandal demonstrated that corrupt links between politics and business were still deeply entrenched.
Prosecutors said banks pressured by politicians offered loans in return for kickbacks from Hanbo Steel, which racked up $5.8 billion in debt before going under on January 23.

Political analysts said Kim, with his political gambler's instincts, would almost certainly make dramatic efforts to win back support before presidential elections in December. He did not unveil any fresh initiatives on Tuesday.
Kim is constitutionally barred from seeking another term, but is eager to install a protege in office to shield him in his retirement.
Opposition parties have demanded a new probe, saying state prosecutors failed to uncover the "real big hands" in a scandal that has eaten into Kim's political credibility.
A recent survey by the monthly magazine WIN showed that about 73 percent of those polled believed the president's reforms had failed.

The president's reformist image also has been tarnished by a controversial labour law, rammed through parliament in a dawn session that recalled the tactics of his military predecessors. A hawkish stance against North Korea and a crackdown on student protests have further eroded his popularity.
Kim's popularity, which topped 90 percent as he began his anti-graft campaign in 1993, is now hovering around 10 percent.
The WIN survey showed 70 percent of those polled thought Kim himself might have to be probed over the loan scandal.

Among the successes of Kim's term has been the prosecution and jailing of his two predecessors Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo for corruption and human rights abuses. Chun is now serving a life sentence and Roh a 17-year jail term.
